newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- US Dec housing starts seen retreating.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- US Dec housing starts seen retreating.

text.p: U.S. housing starts probably declined in December after a November surge, fitting the view that housing activity has plateaued but at fairly healthy levels, economists said.
In a Reuters poll, economists forecast, on average, that housing starts fell to an annualized rate of 1.470 million in December from 1.514 million in November.
The data are due to be released on Wednesday, January 22 at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Economists at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp estimated that housing starts fell 3.0 percent to 1.47 million during December.
But that decline follows a 9.2 percent surge in starts during November and economists say housing activity is far from moribund.
"By and large, housing has held up better than we had expected," said economists at Chase Securities Inc in a recent research release.

Chase forecast a decline in overall housing starts to 1.45 million in December, saying that poor weather on the West Coast likely curbed housing activity in that part of the nation. Also, housing starts in the South probably reverted to trend, after a strong showing in November, Chase said.

Smith Barney economist William Sharp looks for a smaller decline in December housing starts. When the data are released, Sharp believes they will show a two percent decline to a 1.484 million unit pace in December.
"Our prediction assumes a 2.5 percent decline in single-family starts and a modest 0.3 percent decline in multifamily starts," he said.
Single-family units account for about 80 percent of total housing starts.
BancAmerica Securities Inc economist Steven Wood also looks for an annualized 1.48 million starts for December.
"Recent strength in new home sales should help support new construction although at levels modestly lower than in November," said Wood.
Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette economist Marilyn Schaja said the rate of housing starts has hit a plateau.
"The (1.51 annualized) rate of starts in November was unsustainable," she said.
